clf-med-031.text: An order-processing application runs on one large EC2 instance. During sales peaks, the team increases the instance size from m5.large to m5.4xlarge, which requires a restart and eventually reaches hardware limits. The architect proposes adding more smaller instances behind a load balancer as demand grows. Which scalability approach is being proposed?
options: Replace high availability with fault tolerance
Replace vertical scaling (scale up) with horizontal scaling (scale out)
Replace on-demand provisioning with advance capacity provisioning
Replace horizontal scaling (scale out) with vertical scaling (scale up)
clf-med-031.explanation: Increasing the size of one instance is vertical scaling, or scale up, which is bounded by the largest available hardware and may require disruption. Adding more instances in parallel is horizontal scaling, or scale out, which is typically more elastic and resilient in cloud architectures.
clf-med-031.hint: Compare making one machine larger with adding more machines side by side. These are the two classic scaling directions.
optionRationales: Increasing the size of one instance is vertical scaling, or scale up, which is bounded by the largest available hardware and may require disruption. Adding more instances in parallel is horizontal scaling, or scale out, which is typically more elastic and resilient in cloud architectures.
This reverses the scenario: increasing the size of an instance is vertical scaling, while adding more instances is horizontal scaling.
High availability and fault tolerance are resilience properties, not the names of the two capacity-scaling strategies described here.
The proposal moves away from advance fixed provisioning because instances are added as demand grows.

clf-med-032.text: An operations team wants an AWS tool that continuously evaluates an account and provides automatic recommendations in categories such as cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits, and operational excellence by comparing the environment against AWS best practices. Which tool provides these automated checks?
options: AWS Health Dashboard
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon CloudWatch
AWS Well-Architected Tool
clf-med-032.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor inspects supported aspects of an AWS environment and provides recommendations based on AWS best practices across categories such as cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service quotas, and operational excellence.
clf-med-032.hint: Think of the automated AWS advisor that highlights waste, security risks, performance opportunities, and quota concerns.
optionRationales: AWS Trusted Advisor inspects supported aspects of an AWS environment and provides recommendations based on AWS best practices across categories such as cost optimization, performance, security, fault tolerance, service quotas, and operational excellence.
AWS Well-Architected Tool guides structured workload reviews against framework pillars rather than automatically inspecting account resources in the same way as Trusted Advisor.
Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms for operational monitoring but is not primarily a best-practice recommendation service.
AWS Health Dashboard reports AWS service events and account-specific health information but does not perform broad best-practice optimization checks.

clf-med-033.text: A traditional retail network takes on average 10 weeks to provide a new server for your developers, between purchase, delivery and configuration. After migrating to AWS, the same provisioning went on to take minutes, allowing to test new ideas quickly, fail cheap and launch products before competitors. What benefit of cloud computing this contrast evidences?
options: Fault tolerance: continuing to operate despite failed components
Economies of scale: obtaining lower prices from AWS aggregate purchasing power
Agility: increasing experimentation and innovation speed by reducing resource-provisioning time
Durability: guaranteeing that data is never lost
clf-med-033.explanation: Cloud agility turns weeks of infrastructure waiting time into minutes, accelerating experimentation, reducing the cost of failed attempts, and shortening time to market.
clf-med-033.hint: The key contrast is time: from weeks to minutes between requesting infrastructure and having it available for innovation.
optionRationales: Cloud agility turns weeks of infrastructure waiting time into minutes, accelerating experimentation, reducing the cost of failed attempts, and shortening time to market.
Durability refers to data protection and persistence over time (such as 11 of the S3), and not at the speed of provisioning and innovation.
Economies of scale refer to lower unit costs produced by AWS aggregate purchasing and operations scale, not shorter provisioning cycles.
Fault tolerance is the ability to continue operating despite component failures and is unrelated to rapid resource provisioning for experimentation.

clf-med-034.text: An application running on an Amazon EC2 instance needs to read and write objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. A developer proposes storing an IAM user's access keys in the application code, but the security team rejects the idea. According to AWS best practices, how should these permissions be granted?
options: Use the account root user's credentials so no permission is missing
Store permanent access keys in an encrypted configuration file on the instance
Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance so the application receives temporary credentials automatically
Make the S3 bucket public so the instance can access it without authentication
clf-med-034.explanation: The recommended approach is to use an IAM role for the workload. A role associated with the EC2 instance through an instance profile provides temporary credentials that AWS rotates automatically, avoiding long-lived keys embedded in code.
clf-med-034.hint: Best practice for granting permissions to workloads rather than people uses temporary credentials delivered automatically.
optionRationales: The recommended approach is to use an IAM role for the workload. A role associated with the EC2 instance through an instance profile provides temporary credentials that AWS rotates automatically, avoiding long-lived keys embedded in code.
Even when encrypted, long-lived keys stored on the instance remain static credentials requiring manual rotation and are less secure than temporary credentials from IAM roles.
Root credentials should never be embedded in applications because they provide unrestricted account access and would create catastrophic exposure if compromised.
Making the bucket public would expose data broadly to solve an internal authentication requirement and would violate fundamental security practices.

clf-med-035.text: An administrator needs to allow a partner AWS account to access objects in one company S3 bucket. The permission is configured directly on the bucket by specifying the partner account as an allowed principal in a JSON policy attached to the resource. What type of IAM policy is being used?
options: A resource-based policy, such as an S3 bucket policy
An identity-based policy attached to an IAM user
An AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP)
A Network Access Control List (Network ACL)
clf-med-035.explanation: Resource-based policies are attached directly to resources such as S3 buckets and specify which principals, including principals in other AWS accounts, can access the resource.
clf-med-035.hint: The policy is attached to the resource itself, not to a user or group. That determines the policy category.
optionRationales: Resource-based policies are attached directly to resources such as S3 buckets and specify which principals, including principals in other AWS accounts, can access the resource.
Identity-based policies are attached to IAM users, groups, or roles and define what those identities can do; they are not attached directly to the bucket as described.
SCPs define permission guardrails for accounts in AWS Organizations. They do not grant access and are not attached to individual resources such as buckets.
Network ACLs filter network traffic at the VPC subnet level and are unrelated to cross-account authorization for S3 objects.

clf-med-036.text: An IAM user has two applicable policies: one allows all Amazon S3 actions, while another contains an explicit Deny for deleting objects from an audit bucket. What happens when the user tries to delete an object from that bucket, and why?
options: The deletion is allowed because the Allow policy was attached first
The deletion is allowed because broader policies override specific policies
The deletion is denied because an explicit Deny overrides any Allow
IAM requests manual administrator confirmation to resolve the conflict
clf-med-036.explanation: In IAM policy evaluation, an applicable explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow. If an explicit Deny applies to an action, that action is denied even when another policy allows it.
clf-med-036.hint: IAM has a fundamental policy-evaluation rule about which effect always wins when Allow and explicit Deny conflict.
optionRationales: In IAM policy evaluation, an applicable explicit Deny takes precedence over an Allow. If an explicit Deny applies to an action, that action is denied even when another policy allows it.
The order of annexation of policies is irrelevant in the evaluation of the IAM; what determines the result is the predence of the explicit Deny over the Allow.
IAM does not use a rule where the broadest policy automatically wins. An explicit applicable Deny blocks the action regardless of Allows.
IAM policy evaluation is automatic and deterministic; there is no manual approval workflow for resolving Allow-versus-Deny conflicts.

clf-med-037.text: A new AWS account administrator has configured IAM users with administrative privileges for day-to-day work but knows that a small number of account-level tasks require root-user credentials. Which action is an example of a task that may require the AWS account root user?
options: Launch and terminate production EC2 instances
Create IAM users and attach permission policies
Perform certain account-level actions such as closing the AWS account
View ordinary resource metrics in Amazon CloudWatch
clf-med-037.explanation: Some sensitive account-level tasks are restricted to the AWS account root user, such as closing the AWS account. Root credentials should therefore be protected with MFA and used only when a task specifically requires them.
clf-med-037.hint: Think of actions that affect the AWS account itself rather than ordinary resources inside the account.
optionRationales: Some sensitive account-level tasks are restricted to the AWS account root user, such as closing the AWS account. Root credentials should therefore be protected with MFA and used only when a task specifically requires them.
IAM users or roles with appropriate permissions can administer IAM resources without using the root user for routine identity-management tasks.
EC2 resource operations are normal administrative tasks that should be performed by appropriately authorized IAM identities rather than the root user.
Operational service access such as viewing CloudWatch data can be delegated through IAM permissions and is not inherently a root-only task.

clf-med-038.text: A company's security policy requires all IAM users with console access to provide a second authentication factor in addition to a password, such as an authenticator application or a physical FIDO security key. Which IAM mechanism meets this requirement?
options: IAM password policy
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Programmatic access keys
clf-med-038.explanation: MFA adds another authentication factor beyond the password, such as an authenticator application or hardware security key, reducing the risk from stolen passwords.
clf-med-038.hint: The requirement combines something the user knows with something the user has. That is the key authentication concept.
optionRationales: MFA adds another authentication factor beyond the password, such as an authenticator application or hardware security key, reducing the risk from stolen passwords.
A password policy can enforce password complexity and other password controls but still operates around a single knowledge factor.
Access keys are credentials for programmatic access and are not a second factor for console authentication.
The ACM certified management TLS/SSL for encryption of application connections, without any role in authentication of users on the console.

clf-med-039.text: A holding uses the AWS Organizations and applied a Service Control Policy (SCP) which blocks the use of regions outside Brazil in the accounts of the organizational production unit. An administrator of one of these accounts has a policy that IAM with total access (AdministratorAccess), but when trying to create resources in another region it gets denied access. Why this happens?
options: The administrator must enable MFA before using other Regions
SCPs grant additional permissions and the correct SCP has not yet been attached
The administrator's IAM policy is corrupted and must be reattached
SCPs define the account's maximum permission boundary, so actions restricted by the SCP remain unavailable even to identities with broad IAM permissions
clf-med-039.explanation: SCPs act as organization-level guardrails that define the maximum available permissions for member accounts. IAM policies inside an account cannot grant access beyond what the applicable SCPs permit.
clf-med-039.hint: Think of the hierarchy: an action restricted by the organization-level guardrail cannot be re-enabled by a policy inside the member account.
optionRationales: SCPs act as organization-level guardrails that define the maximum available permissions for member accounts. IAM policies inside an account cannot grant access beyond what the applicable SCPs permit.
The IAM policy can remain valid while the effective permission evaluation is constrained by an SCP at the organization level.
SCPs do not grant permissions by themselves; they restrict the permissions that IAM policies can effectively authorize in member accounts.
MFA is an authentication factor and is unrelated to a Region restriction imposed by an organization SCP.

clf-med-040.text: An e-commerce company faces sophisticated recurring DDoS attacks and wants more than the default automatic protection. It also requires access to AWS specialized DDoS response expertise, advanced detection, and cost protection for scaling charges caused by attacks. Which AWS service is designed for these requirements?
options: AWS Shield Standard
AWS Shield Advanced
Amazon Inspector
Amazon GuardDuty
clf-med-040.explanation: The Shield Advanced offers, in addition to protection of Shield Standard, advanced DDoS attack detection, access to response team (Shield Response Team), financial protection against cost peaks caused by attacks and integration with the AWS WAF without additional cost.
clf-med-040.hint: Specialized response assistance and cost protection point to the paid advanced tier of AWS DDoS protection.
optionRationales: The Shield Advanced offers, in addition to protection of Shield Standard, advanced DDoS attack detection, access to response team (Shield Response Team), financial protection against cost peaks caused by attacks and integration with the AWS WAF without additional cost.
The Shield Standard is free and automatic against common layer attacks 3 and 4, but does not include dedicated response team, advanced detection or financial protection.
Amazon GuardDuty detects suspicious behavior by analyzing security telemetry but is not the primary DDoS mitigation and response service.
The Inspector checks software vulnerabilities and network exposure in workloads (EC2, ECR, Lambda), without any DDoS attack mitigation function.
